rv.q: There are diaphanous curtains and shabby chic furniture along with Laura’s glass menagerie, which twirls like a multi-tiered cake platter above her phonograph. An otherworldly beauty is mixed with grit and grime, such as the mound of sand amid the furniture, sprinkled with glitter and with flowers growing in it.

Making his professional debut, Jad Sayegh projects self-confidence as Tom’s go-getting work colleague, Jim, but makes clear the self-doubt and desperate need for validation behind the assured mask. But it’s another debut, in Eva Morgan’s touching turn as fragile wallflower Laura, that really stands out.
“We reimagine theatre to reimagine the world” runs the mission-statement of The Yard in Hackney Wick. A grand claim. But weighing the evidence of the past 14 years, the vaunt seems amply justified.

Yet, as director Jay Miller points out in the programme, it is a play about “what we remember and how we remember it and whether we can ever leave our memories behind.” In that context of holding on and letting go, it is suddenly the perfect choice. Miller gives it a fiercely anti-naturalistic production that suits the aesthetic of his theatre.
